newsitem.title: BRAZIL: U.S. disappointed at Brazil move on anti-drugs aid.
newsitem.headline: U.S. disappointed at Brazil move on anti-drugs aid.

text.p: Brazil has rejected as "laughable" the $600,000 offered by Washington to fight the drugs war, a decision met with disappointment on Tuesday by the U.S. Embassy in Brasilia.

A spokeswoman for Brazilian Justice Minister Nelson Jobim said he decided over the weekend to refuse the aid. Newspapers reported he considered the sum derisory and had also broken off talks with the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration over cooperation.
"U.S.-Brazilian relations have never been better," the U.S. embassy said in a statement.

"In this context, we were surprised and disappointed to read in the media comments by (Brazilian) officials questioning the utility of a longstanding U.S. programme of cooperation and assistance in combating drug abuse and trafficking."

The $600,000 was offered to Brazil to help fight the drug trade next year. The U.S. Embassy said it was part of a longstanding programme to which Washington had contributed about $16 million over the past 22 years.

"Minister Jobim ordered the money be rejected," his spokeswoman said. O Globo newspaper said Jobim had halted talks with the DEA over cooperation in the drug war because "there's no point in talking over this amount of money."
Jobim's decision was reportedly supported by President Fernando Henrique Cardoso. Both the Presidential Palace and the Foreign Ministry declined to comment.
Brazilian officials said that last year, the DEA gave $20 million to neighbouring Colombia.
They said that Brazil, as a major transshipment route if not producer of cocaine from Bolivia, Peru and Colombia, should be helped to a similar extent.
"We are no longer going to follow the DEA policy of erecting a wall only to prevent drugs entering the United States without caring for the countries through which the drugs pass," Jobim told Globo.
Experts say the flow of drugs through the Amazon river basin has been gaining pace as Colombia cracks down on its cartels.
The Brazilian Federal Police patrol the myriad rivers of the rain forest, but according to local media reports, their speed boats are largely dry-docked because of a lack of fuel.
The U.S. Embassy said it had always considered the programme with Brazil to be part of an overall international effort.
It said the $16 million donated over the past 22 years had been directed at training and equipping the Brazilian Federal Police and at fighting internal demand.
It said Washington was not consulted or given advance notice of Jobim's decision.
"For our part, the United States remains ready to cooperate at all levels with Brazil to combat the scourge of drug abuse and trafficking that affects both our countries," it added.
